analysis.one_liner: Bars the federal government from taxing investment gains on assets their owners have not sold.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law that no federal official — including the Treasury Secretary — may impose a tax on unrealized capital gains, meaning increases in the value of stocks, businesses, or other assets that the owner has not yet sold. Today such gains are generally taxed only when sold; this bill would lock that in and rule out any future tax on paper wealth. It was introduced by Rep. Byron Donalds with 10 Republican cosponsors and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthiest households whose wealth sits in stocks, businesses, and other assets that grow in value without being sold. The bill would permanently shield those gains from any federal tax, while wages are taxed as they are earned.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with large unsold investment gains

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Treasury Secretary or any other federal official from imposing or requiring taxation on unrealized capital gains on any taxable asset, including gifts, bequests, and transfers in trust [S3].
It would bar not just a current proposal but any future effort to tax wealth gains before sale, converting today's practice into a permanent legal shield [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If such a tax were ever needed to raise revenue, the burden would stay on workers whose income is taxed when earned, and on anyone who benefits from government services funded by that revenue — the bill forecloses one way of asking the largest asset holders to contribute.

drawbacks.text: An honest supporter's cost: by ruling out taxation of unrealized gains, the bill preserves a system where a person can hold appreciating assets for life and never pay tax on that growth, while salaried workers pay tax on every paycheck [S3].
The bill would tie the hands of future Congresses, preventing any majority from choosing mark-to-market taxation as a revenue option without first repealing this prohibition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers certainty to large asset holders and forecloses a revenue tool aimed almost entirely at the top of the wealth distribution. Its cost falls diffuse: whatever a future unrealized-gains tax might have raised would have to come from other taxpayers or borrowed funds. There is no offsetting benefit for ordinary workers in the bill text.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Byron Donalds introduced the bill on November 2, 2021, during debate over proposals to tax large unrealized gains [S1].
Ten Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further action — no markup, no hearing, no floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed in practice: the bill died, and no unrealized-gains tax passed either, so the wealthiest asset holders kept the existing rule that paper gains go untaxed until sold. Ordinary taxpayers neither gained nor lost anything concrete, but the door to that tax closed with the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large asset holders kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Byron Donalds
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit federal taxation of unrealized capital gains.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — letting the bill expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was Republican; no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved the bill.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households with large unrealized gains
industries.note: The bill would permanently shield gains on unsold stocks, businesses, and trusts from federal tax. Its benefit flows from keeping a revenue option away from the top of the wealth distribution, leaving the burden on wage earners.
By extending the prohibition to gifts, bequests, and transfers in trust, the bill would lock in the advantage of holding appreciated assets across generations, the market that estate planners serve.
